Learning Objectives
Describe the anatomy, structure, composition, and biomechanics of the hip labrum.
Describe the vascularization of the hip labrum.
Assess injury patterns and the healing capacity of the hip labrum.
Perform an appropriate workup for patients in whom a torn labrum is suspected.
Determine the surgical management of labral tears.
Structure and Composition of the Hip Labrum
Anatomy
The horseshoe-shaped structure continues with the transverse acetabular ligament.



Anchored at the non-articular and articular side of the rim
Chondrolabral complex

Anatomy
The anatomic configuration of the acetabular labrum corresponds with the structure of
the bony acetabulum. The acetabulum has a rounded shape with a mean diameter of 52
mm (± 4 mm);1 however, sex- and race-dependent variations exist.2,3 The acetabulum
has a peripheral horseshoe-shaped articulating surface lined with cartilage and a central
cotyloid fossa filled with the round ligament (teres ligament) surrounded by fatty tissue
over a synovial membrane (ie, pulvinar). The most distal aspect of the acetabulum
(acetabular notch) becomes a foramen by the presence of the transverse acetabular
ligament.1,4 In addition, the transverse acetabular ligament is reported to show
continuity anteriorly and posteriorly with the most dense and flattened collagen fibers of
the labrum.5,6
The labrum is a dense fibroelastic tissue with a triangular shape that embraces the bony
rim in an almost 360° fashion, increasing the acetabular volume by 30%.7 The labrum is
anchored to the nonarticular side of the rim and to the articular aspect indirectly
through a thin area of calcified cartilage (ie, transitional zone or chondrolabral region;
Figure 1). It is wider in its anterior one-half and thickest in its superior one-half.6 This
correlates with the articular acetabular cartilage thickness, which is denser
superolaterally (mean thickness of 1.83 mm compared with a mean thickness of 1.26
mm in the rest of the acetabulum).8 The labrum is externally surrounded by a robust
joint capsule that also attaches to the acetabular rim, outwardly to the labral attachment
(Figure 1).

Figure 1 Illustration of the acetabular labrum. The inset shows the posterior labral fiber
configuration, with fibers running perpendicular to the cartilage area, depicting a more
robust labral attachment than the one observed anteriorly (with fibers running parallel
to cartilage). (Courtesy of Franco L. De Cicco, MD, Buenos Aires, Argentina.)
Microscopically, the chondrolabral complex consists of seven different types of
connective tissue, as described by Field and Rajakulendran9: articular cartilage, labrum,
bone, blood vessels, nerve fibers, synovium, and capsule. The 1- to 2-mm area from
which the hyaline cartilage turns into acetabular labrum, termed the transitional area,
can be distinguished anteriorly and posteriorly by a different fiber disposition. The
anterior collagen fibers of the labrum are parallel to those of the bony edge. Therefore,
this attachment is easily subject to separation from shear forces. Posteriorly, the fibers
attach perpendicular to the edge and merge with the collagen fibers of the bony edge
and, therefore, are resistant to tearing10 (Figure 2).

Labral Vascularization
Ring of circulation from the periacetabular vascular ring
Predominantly from superior and inferior gluteal arteries
Located on the capsular surface

Labral Vascularization
The labrum receives vascularization from the periacetabular vascular ring, which is
composed of radial branches that mainly derive from the superior and inferior gluteal
arteries; however, some distal vascularization also originates from the medial and lateral
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:23 PM
AAOS | Hip Labrum
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001153
4/18

femoral circumflex arteries.11 The vascular ring is located on the capsular surface of the
labrum. The highest vascular concentration is located at the posterior one-half of the
labrum.11 Such branches penetrate the capsule through its innominate (ie, bony)
insertion and run perpendicular to the osseolabral complex, ending near the free edge
of the labrum. Therefore, the labrum has two distinct vascular zones: the extra-articular
zone, which is well vascularized around dense connective tissue, and the intra-articular
zone, which is largely avascular.12 Vascular anatomy has important implications in
deciding between débridement or repair.13 Regardless, additional research on the
healing capacity of the labrum in relation to its vascular supply is required to better
delineate the reason some hips with structural bony deficiency (ie, hip dysplasia) may
benefit from realignment osteotomy with or without concomitant open or arthroscopic
labral repair14,15 (Figure 3).
Figure 3 Anterior and posterior view illustrations show the periacetabular vascular ring.
The inset shows the location of the perivascular ring at the capsular surface of the
labrum. (Courtesy of Franco L. De Cicco, MD, Buenos Aires, Argentina.)

Biomechanical Properties
Primary hip stabilizer to distraction forces (suction seal)
Provides joint homeostasis
Decreases cartilage contact pressure

Biomechanical Properties
Hip joint intrinsic stability relies on three constant structures: osseous anatomy, the
acetabular labrum, and the surrounding capsuloligamentous complex. If one of these
structures is damaged or malfunctioning, the other structures are required to
compensate; however, if physiologic loads continue, the compensation mechanism will
eventually fail, resulting in chondrolabral damage.16 The acetabular labrum plays a key
role in maintaining hip joint homeostasis for its numerous functions: stability, load
distribution, regulation of the synovial fluid, proprioception, and maintenance of intra-
articular negative pressure (suction seal).17,18 These functions, more specifically the
latter, help distribute continuous compressive loads in a uniform fashion, consequently
reducing cartilage stress. Fluid circulation inside the joint is leveled at the junction of the
labrum and femoral head. Resistance to fluid passage from the central compartment
depends on the integrity of the labrum. In addition, the labrum increases the contact
area of the hip joint, which decreases cartilage contact pressure.19 The smaller (<6 mm)
the height of the acetabulum, the shorter the distance to break the suction seal and
decrease peak negative pressure.20 This shows the manner in which the labrum
contributes to the distractive stability of the hip. Removal of the labrum results in less
intra-articular hip contact area and loss of suction seal.21 A radial tear in the acetabular
labrum decreases adjacent labral strain; however, removal of 2 cm or more of the
acetabular labrum is necessary before hip stability decreases.22 Therefore, most hip
preservation surgeons tend to preserve and repair the labrum rather than perform
resection.
Biology


Biology
Few data are available on the ultrastructure and metabolism of the acetabular labrum.
The labrum has three layers: the surface layer, which has collagen fibers; the middle
layer with fibrocartilage in which cartilage tissue is embedded; and the deep layer,
composed mainly of blood vessels.23 Scanning electron microscopy shows that collagen
fibers are mostly thin type I collagen fibers (superficial layer), with a mean diameter of
155.63 nm (± 25.48 nm), whereas chondrocytes (middle layer) have a broad cytoplasm
around a spindle-shaped central nucleus.24 Findings of a 2012 study in which
investigators compared cell morphology and metabolism of human articular
chondrocytes, meniscal cells, and acetabular labrum cells showed that expression of
COL1A1 was higher in meniscal and labral cells than in chondrocytes.25 Morphology of
the labral cell was similar to that of the meniscal cell. Expression of COL2A1 was greater
in the labral cells than in meniscal cells. Compared with cartilage, labral and meniscal
cells expressed higher levels of proinflammatory interleukin-6 and extracellular matrix–
degrading enzymes (matrix metalloproteinases 1, 2, and9 and a disintegrin and
metalloproteinase with thrombospondin motifs 4) under the effects of interleukin-1 (a
known driver of inflammatory joint disease).25 This shows a potentially direct
relationship between the genesis of arthritic changes and labral tears.
Injury, Repair, and Healing
Tears rarely occur in isolation.
Secondary most commonly to femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) or developmental
dysplasia of the hip
Seldes classification system
Labral healing capacity remains controversial.

Injury, Repair, and Healing
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:23 PM
AAOS | Hip Labrum
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001153
7/18

Labral tears infrequently occur in isolation. They usually are identified in patients with
underlying structural abnormalities (ie, FAI or dysplasia).12 Lage et al26 categorized the
etiology of labral tears into four groups: traumatic (traction or hyperrotation injury),
congenital (eg, dysplasia), degenerative (eg, arthritis), and idiopathic (no clear cause). In
addition, Lage et al26 described a morphologic classification system (radial flap, radial
fibrillated, longitudinal peripheral, and unstable; Figure 4).
Figure 4 Illustration shows the morphology of labral tears. (Courtesy of Franco L. De
Cicco, MD, Buenos Aires, Argentina.)
Seldes et al6 further characterized different types of labral injuries according to the
underlying osseous abnormality leading to FAI. Cam-type FAI damages the chondrolabral
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:23 PM
AAOS | Hip Labrum
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001153
8/18

junction by detaching the labrum from the articular side (Seldes type 1 tear), also
affecting peripheral cartilage and occasionally extending into the subchondral bone.27
Pincer-type FAI from acetabular overcoverage repetitively crushes the labrum alongside
the femoral head-neck junction, producing one or more cleavage planes within the
substance of the labrum but typically not disrupting the chondrolabral junction (Seldes
type 2 tear). Both types of injuries occur in an outside-in direction, whereas labral lesions
in patients with hip dysplasia characteristically develop inside out, usually separating the
rim from the labrum,28 given the incapacity of the femoral head to maintain its
centralization at the native center of rotation29 (Figure 5).
Figure 5 Illustrations show the Seldes classification, which is based on the underlying
osseous abnormality. A, Normal labrum. B, The outside-in type of labrum tear
commonly observed in patients with a Cam lesion. C, The outside-in type of labrum tear
commonly observed in patients with a pincer lesion. D, The inside-out labral tear
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:23 PM
AAOS | Hip Labrum
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001153
9/18

commonly observed in patients with hip dysplasia. (Courtesy of Franco L. De Cicco, MD,
Buenos Aires, Argentina.)
The most commonly used labral tear classification system was described by Beck et al27
in 2005, and includes a combination of both previously mentioned classification systems.
This includes the following morphologies: normal (sound labrum); degeneration
(thinning or localized hypertrophy, fraying, discoloration); full-thickness tear (complete
avulsion from the rim); detachment (separation between acetabular and labral cartilage);
and ossification (localized or diffuse osseous metaplasia).27 In addition, labral lesions are
labeled with numbers that correlate with their spatial position.
Modern open and arthroscopic management consists of labral repair with suture
anchors if possible. The healing capacity of the labrum remains a controversial issue.
Because the articular side of the labrum has minimal vascularization, some surgeons
believe that the innate potential for repair is close to absent;30 however, evidence from
retrieved biopsy specimens from ovine models and human cases show signs of
neovascularization in the proximity of the sutures after labral repair, via fibrovascular
repair tissue, or directly via new bone formation.6,31,32
Diagnosis and Management of Labral Tears
Clinical Examination
C sign
Provocative tests
Bilateral assessment of hip range of motion

Clinical Examination
A thorough patient history and physical examination are critical to achieve an accurate
diagnosis and, therefore, determine an appropriate treatment strategy. Patient age,
history of trauma, sports injuries, prior treatments, and previous functional limitations
should be carefully evaluated. Other symptoms, such as back pain, weakness, radiating
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:23 PM
AAOS | Hip Labrum
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001153
10/18

pain or numbness, night pain, and bilateral groin pain may help rule out spinal
pathology. Typically, patients describe hip pain as a deep interior hip pain, often pointing
with one finger or making the typical C sign.
Range of motion is key in distinguishing a loose hip (ie, unstable, as in hip dysplasia)
from a rigid hip (ie, constrained, as in FAI).33 Commonly, dysplasia is observed in young
female patients who have a loose joint. Pain commonly is exacerbated if the patient
stands for long hours, and it is located laterally at the end of the day (abductor muscle
fatigue). Contrarily, FAI is most observed in young active males and is worse if the patient
sits for long hours (flexion of the hip). Provocative maneuvers include the FADIR (pain
with hip flexion, adduction, and internal rotation) test and the FABER (pain with hip
flexion, abduction, and external rotation) test. Diagnostic injections have been used as
an adjunct in the diagnosis of intra-articular hip pathology.34
Radiographic Workup
AP radiograph of the pelvis (standing position)
Dunn radiograph and frog lateral radiograph (assess head-neck offset anteriorly)
Confirms etiology (developmental dysplasia of the hip, FAI, sequelae of childhood disease)
Magnetic resonance arthrography (MRA) is the preferred imaging modality to confirm labral
tears.

Radiographic Workup
A standard AP radiograph of the pelvis provides valuable information on the morphology
of the acetabulum, including signs and severity of dysplasia, acetabular overcoverage,
retroversion, protrusion, and profunda. The joint space can be evaluated on this view
and graded according to the Tönnis classification.35 Various angles—including the lateral
center to edge, the Tönnis angle, and the alpha angle—are commonly used to diagnose
primary pathology. Ossification of the labrum and rim fractures (os acetabuli) often also
can be appreciated on this view. Dunn and frog lateral views allow the clinician to
evaluate the head-neck deformity located in the anterior aspect of the femoral neck. A
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:23 PM
AAOS | Hip Labrum
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001153
11/18

45° Dunn lateral view (obtained with the patient supine with neutral pelvic rotation and
the hip flexed 45° and abducted 20°) highly correlates with radial oblique MRI/CT scans
and, therefore, is useful in detecting femoral head-neck junction malformation at the
most typical 1:30 clock-face position on the femoral neck.36,37 If femoral head
asphericity lies more anteriorly (at the 3-o’clock position or beyond), a frog lateral view is
more clinically useful38 (Figure 6).
Figure 6 Pelvic radiographs demonstrates angles measured to evaluate the severity of
hip dysplasia. A, AP radiograph demonstrates the lateral center edge (LCE) and the
Tönnis angle. B, Dunn radiograph demonstrates the alpha angle, which is used to
confirm cam deformity or abnormal head-neck offset. (Courtesy of Cecilia Pascual-
Garrido, MD, PhD, St. Louis, MO.)
In patients in whom intra-articular pathology is suspected, magnetic resonance
arthrography with gadolinium contrast is the preferred imaging modality for the
detection of labral tears. In addition, magnetic resonance arthrography is used to rule
out other disorders, such as stress fractures, osteonecrosis, tumors, and disease or
injury to extra-articular structures (Figure 7).

Management
Nonsurgical management
Surgical management

Management
Initially, a course of nonsurgical management is attempted. This typically consists of
NSAIDs and focused physical therapy for 4 to 6 weeks. Steroid injections may be
indicated, especially in high-level athletes who need to finish a season and postpone
surgery until the off-season.
In patients with FAI, adequate resection of the cam or pincer deformity will prevent
recurrent damage to the labrum. In patients with developmental dysplasia of the hip, a
periacetabular osteotomy will provide protection for the labral repair if undertaken.
Suitability for repair can be determined based on classification and healing potential,
which may be affected by a patient’s age and the location of the tear. If the damage is
deemed extensive enough and sufficient labral tissue is available for repair, then repair
often is undertaken. Currently, labral débridement has lost popularity. Prospective and
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:23 PM
AAOS | Hip Labrum
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001153
13/18

retrospective studies have demonstrated that, although débridement may provide some
improvement in outcome scores, a greater benefit generally is observed in patients who
undergo repair.39,40
If labral repair is undertaken, arthroscopy has become the preferred tool, regardless of
etiology. Various suture anchors are available, including metal anchors, biocomposites,
all-suture, knotless, and traditional knot-tied anchors. The surgeon selects the
appropriate anchor based on the design and material that will best stabilize the labral
base and restore the fluid seal (Figure 8).
Figure 8 Arthroscopic images of a hip show repair of a labrum tear. A, Image shows a
labrum tear with fibrillation. B, Labrum repair was performed with use of knotless
anchors. (Courtesy of Cecilia Pascual-Garrido, MD, PhD, St. Louis, MO.)
